title: William F. Buckley Jr. vs. Gore Vidal on ABC News (August 28, 1968)
context: Authentic reconstruction of the explosive ABC News televised convention debate between conservative commentator William F. Buckley Jr. and liberal novelist-essayist Gore Vidal, moderated by Howard K. Smith during the tumultuous 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago on August 28, 1968. Tracks escalating tension across four rounds: street protests and police violence outside the convention hall, the film footage of protesters raising the Vietcong flag in Grant Park and analogies to Nazi symbolism, mutual accusations of totalitarianism and 'crypto-Nazi' sympathy, and the infamous on-air personal confrontation that ended in Buckley's threat and Howard K. Smith's emergency intervention.

metadata.event: ABC News 1968 Democratic National Convention Debate
key_themes: Police Violence vs. Law and Order
Freedom of Dissent & Vietcong Flag Provocation
metadata.historical_outcome: Culminated in the most famous live television confrontation in American broadcast history ('crypto-Nazi' vs. Buckley's 'queer' threat), triggering decades of defamation litigation and reshaping televised political commentary.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Good evening from Chicago, where tonight's Democratic National Convention unfolds amid violent clashes in the streets between anti-war demonstrators and Mayor Daley's police outside the amphitheater. Joining ABC News for our nightly commentary are Mr. William F. Buckley Jr. and Mr. Gore Vidal. Let us begin with the scenes we have just watched from Michigan Avenue and Grant Park: who bears primary responsibility for the breakdown of order in Chicago?

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Howard, one must first acknowledge the extraordinary provocation inflicted upon the city of Chicago by organized bands of radical agitators who came here expressly to disrupt a constitutional convention, hurl obscenities and projectiles at policemen, and provoke a televised confrontation. While individual excesses by police officers must be condemned wherever they occur, no civilized society can allow militant mobs to paralyze a major American city or intimidate delegates inside the convention hall.

turns.speaker: Gore Vidal
turns.text: Bill speaks as though young Americans protesting an immoral war in Vietnam arrived here armed like stormtroopers, when in reality we have just witnessed a police riot ordered by Mayor Daley! Television viewers across the country watched uniformed officers beat unarmed demonstrators, club journalists, and gas citizens simply exercising their constitutional right to dissent against a bankrupt war and a rigged party apparatus.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Mr. Vidal, in the film we just saw from Grant Park, some demonstrators pulled down the American flag and attempted to raise the Vietcong flag while American soldiers are fighting and dying in Vietnam. Wasn't it a deliberate, provocative act to raise the Vietcong flag—just as raising the Nazi flag during World War II would have provoked violent outrage?

turns.speaker: Gore Vidal
turns.text: It is hardly the same thing, Howard. The United States is not fighting a declared world war against Hitler's Germany; we are engaged in an undeclared civil war in Southeast Asia that millions of Americans regard as disastrous and unjust. Raising a flag in a public park—however foolish or tasteless—is symbolic political dissent protected by the First Amendment, whereas meeting symbolic speech with nightsticks and cracked skulls is the hallmark of a police state.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: That comparison is morally obtuse! During World War II, raising the swastika in Times Square while American boys bled in Normandy would rightly have been treated as intolerable treasonable provocation against a free republic—and waving the banner of an enemy killing American soldiers in Vietnam similarly forfeits any claim to innocent peaceful dissent. Free speech does not license revolutionary disruption, intimidation, and contempt for lawful authority.

turns.speaker: Gore Vidal
turns.text: Wait a second—you talk about lawful authority and free speech, Bill, yet the real threat to American democracy is not a handful of kids in Grant Park, it is the police-state mentality spreading through this country and encouraged by right-wing apologists like yourself! We have seen authoritarian crackdowns against protesters, minorities, and political dissidents justified endlessly in the name of order.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Now, let us exact a measure of decorum here! Do not start throwing around words like 'police state' or implying sympathy with totalitarianism or Nazism. Some people were indeed pro-Nazi before Pearl Harbor, and let us keep historical truth clear—the American people who oppose mob violence in Chicago are defending constitutional order against anarchic totalitarians of the Left.

turns.speaker: Gore Vidal
turns.text: Shut up a minute—you accuse anyone criticizing police violence of totalitarianism, when as far as I am concerned, the only sort of pro- or crypto-Nazi I can think of is yourself!

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Gentlemen, let us not call names—let us keep this discussion on the issues in Chicago and the protests.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Now listen, you queer, stop calling me a crypto-Nazi or I will sock you in your goddamn face, and you will stay plastered!

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Let us stop calling names and get back to the debate—gentlemen, please, this is a national broadcast!

turns.speaker: Gore Vidal
turns.text: To which remark, there is no reply. The viewer has just witnessed the exact authoritarian temper against which the protesters in Chicago were warning.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: No civilized discourse is possible with someone who casually smears an opponent as a crypto-Nazi on national television while apologizing for street chaos. Let us return to the convention floor.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Gentlemen, our time for tonight's ABC News convention commentary is up. We return to coverage of the Democratic National Convention in Chicago.
